analysis.one_liner: Created a 35% tax bracket for top incomes and repealed a surcharge on middle incomes.
analysis.headline: Introduced with zero cosponsors in October 1990, the bill never left the Ways and Means Committee and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the individual income tax tables to add a new 35% rate on the highest incomes, replacing the then-top rate structure. It would repeal the phaseout that gradually took away the 15% rate and personal exemptions from middle- and upper-middle-income taxpayers, effectively raising their taxes. And it would cap the tax rate on capital gains at 28%, so investment gains would not be taxed at the new 35% top rate.
analysis.who_benefits: Middle- and upper-middle-income taxpayers gain from the repeal of the phaseout of the 15% rate and personal exemptions, which currently raises their effective tax rate [S2][S3]. The federal treasury gains from the new 35% bracket on high incomes, which falls on taxpayers above roughly $47,000 for singles and $78,400 for joint filers [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the phaseout of the 15-percent rate and personal exemptions, a provision that pushes middle- and upper-middle-income taxpayers into higher effective rates.
Creates a 35 percent bracket on the highest incomes, so top earners pay more of the tax burden.

analysis.who_pays: High-income taxpayers, particularly those with wage and salary income, would pay more under the new 35% bracket [S3]. Investors with large capital gains are partially spared, because the bill caps the tax on gains at 28% even while ordinary income reaches 35% [S3].

drawbacks.text: Raising the top marginal rate to 35% would increase taxes on high earners, an approach critics said could discourage work and investment at the margin.
The bill caps capital gains at 28% even as ordinary income reaches 35%, so households living on investment gains would pay a lower rate than many high-earning workers.
The bill text contains drafting inconsistencies in the new rate tables, such as mismatched threshold figures in the rate brackets, which would have needed correction before enactment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill shifts tax burden from middle-income households (by repealing the phaseout) to the highest earners (through the 35% bracket), which is a straightforward redistribution with modest complexity cost. Its main design weakness is the 28% capital gains cap, which leaves investment income taxed more lightly than work income at the top. As a one-page rate rewrite, it is simpler than most tax bills, but its tables needed technical fixes.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in early January 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. William Coyne (D-PA) introduced the bill on October 19, 1990, in the final weeks of the 101st Congress.
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation.
No other member cosponsored the bill.
The committee never held a markup or reported the bill; the final entry in its action history, dated November 5, 1990, simply cross-references a separate bill, H.R. 5835.
The bill never received a floor vote, and the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 with the bill still in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-income taxpayers came out ahead: the 35% top bracket and the related rate restructuring never happened, so the existing top-rate structure stayed in place for the rest of the tax year and beyond.

for.name: Rep. William J. Coyne
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to Ways and Means; no other member joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: Dan Rostenkowski
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee took no action on the bill after referral; it was never marked up or reported to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so the partisan shape of support and opposition cannot be measured from the record.

industries.note: The bill creates a 35% bracket on top incomes, directly raising their taxes. Their interest in blocking the bill ran against middle-income taxpayers, who would have gained from the phaseout repeal.

The bill caps the tax on capital gains at 28%, sparing investment income from the new 35% rate even though ordinary income would reach it. That keeps a preference for gains over wages at the top of the income scale.
